title: Defuse the Bomb
description: Brute force to optimized: separate positive/negative-k logic versus a single normalized direction-and-step loop for circular neighbor summing.

blocks.text: You have a bomb to defuse, represented by a circular array of integers code and a key k. Replace every element of code with a new value: if k is positive, the sum of the next k elements (wrapping around); if k is negative, the sum of the previous k elements, using the absolute value of k (also wrapping around); if k is 0, replace every element with 0. Return the decrypted array.

blocks.caption: Each position sums its k circular neighbors, in the direction k indicates

blocks.text: Given a circular array code and a key k, replace every element with the sum of its k neighbors in the direction indicated by the sign of k, or with 0 everywhere if k is 0.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading Values Off a Circular Dial
blocks.text: Like standing at each mark of a circular dial and reading off the sum of the next few marks clockwise (or the previous few, counter-clockwise), wrapping back to the start once you pass the top of the dial.

blocks.caption: Look ahead or behind by k positions on a circle, wrapping around as needed

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Position 0 sums the next 3 values: 7, 1, 4","12","Since k is positive, look ahead by k positions"],["Position 3 sums the next 3 values, wrapping: 5, 7, 1 (positions 0, 1, 2)","13","Position 3 plus 1 wraps around past the end back to position 0"],["Answer","[12, 10, 16, 13]","Every position's new value is the sum of its next 3 neighbors, wrapping around the circle"]]}

blocks.text: Since k is exactly 0, every position is simply replaced with 0, regardless of the original values.
Since k is negative, each position sums the previous 2 values instead, wrapping backward around the circle when needed, giving [12, 5, 6, 13].
Before writing separate logic for positive and negative k, notice that both cases are really the same operation, just looking in opposite directions.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A positive k means "sum the next k elements", and a negative k means "sum the previous |k| elements" -- these are mirror images of the same task, just with the direction of travel flipped.

Observation 2: Rather than writing two separate code paths, normalize k into a direction (+1 or -1) and a step count (the absolute value of k), then use one shared loop for both cases.

Observation 3: Since the array is circular, any index that runs past the end or before the beginning needs to wrap back around; this is exactly what the modulo operator does, as long as negative results are also corrected back into range.

Observation 4: For each position i, sum the k neighbors found by repeatedly stepping in the chosen direction, wrapping the index with modulo at every step.

Whenever a problem involves a circular array and "looking ahead" or "looking behind" by some fixed count, normalizing the direction once and handling the wraparound with modulo arithmetic keeps the logic simple and shared between cases.
This "normalize the direction, then reuse one shared loop" idea avoids duplicating nearly identical logic for the positive-k and negative-k cases.
For every position, directly sum its k neighbors in the appropriate direction, using modulo arithmetic to wrap the index around the circle.

items: If k is 0, immediately return an array of all zeros, since no summing is needed at all.
Otherwise, for each position, sum either the next k elements (if k is positive) or the previous |k| elements (if k is negative), wrapping indices around the circle with modulo.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The k == 0 case is handled as an immediate early return, since no looping or summing logic applies to it at all.

The positive and negative cases are written as two separate loops here, since the direction of the modulo arithmetic differs slightly between them, even though the ideas are mirror images of each other.
The negative case explicitly adds n before taking modulo, since a raw negative index modulo n in some languages does not automatically wrap into the valid positive range.

blocks.text: Every position's true neighbor sum is computed directly, so the correct decrypted array is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * k), since each of the n positions sums up to k neighbors.
Space: O(n) for the result array (required regardless of approach, since a new array must be returned).

Limitation: with n and k both small (n <= 100), this direct approach is already fast enough in practice, but writing separate logic for the positive and negative cases duplicates nearly identical work.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force works correctly but repeats almost the same logic twice, once for looking ahead and once for looking behind. Since both cases are really "step in some direction, k times, summing as you go", normalizing k into a direction (+1 or -1) and a step count (the absolute value of k) lets a single shared loop handle both cases identically, removing the duplicated logic without changing the overall time complexity.

Determine the direction (+1 if k is positive, -1 if k is negative) and the number of steps (the absolute value of k) once. Then, for every position, sum the values found by repeatedly stepping in that direction, wrapping each index around the circle with modulo.
Normalize the direction and step count once, then reuse a single shared loop for every position, regardless of whether k was originally positive or negative.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * k), the same as the brute force, since the direct nature of the summing doesn't change.
Space: O(n) for the result array.

Normalizing k into a single direction and step count means the exact same loop body correctly handles both the "look ahead" and "look behind" cases, since stepping by -1 repeatedly is identical in structure to stepping by +1 repeatedly, just moving the other way around the circle. The modulo arithmetic, corrected to always land in the valid range [0, n-1], is what makes the wraparound behave correctly regardless of which direction is being used.

items: The direction and step count are computed once, outside the main loop, rather than being re-derived for every position.
The index wraparound formula adds n before taking modulo, guaranteeing a valid non-negative index even when direction is -1 and the raw index would otherwise be negative.
The same inner loop structure is reused for every position, regardless of whether the original k was positive or negative.

blocks.text: When a problem's behavior mirrors itself depending on the sign of some parameter, normalizing that parameter into a direction and a magnitude once often removes a lot of duplicated logic, even without changing the overall time complexity.

items: Forgetting the k == 0 special case, which has no neighbors to sum at all and should immediately return an array of zeros.
Using a raw modulo on a negative index without first adding n, which produces an incorrect negative result in several languages.
Mixing up whether "ahead" means increasing or decreasing index, which flips the direction of the wraparound incorrectly.

items: Mention explicitly that normalizing direction and step count is a general technique for collapsing "mirror image" cases (like positive vs negative offsets) into one shared code path.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Every position in a CIRCULAR array needs a sum of its neighbors ahead or behind, depending on a signed parameter" points toward normalizing that parameter into a direction and magnitude, then using modulo arithmetic (corrected for negative values) to handle the wraparound.

items: How would you make this faster for very large k? A sliding-window-style prefix sum over the doubled (or tripled) circular array could answer every position's neighbor sum in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.

What if the array were not circular, and out-of-range neighbors should simply be ignored? Removing the modulo wraparound and instead clamping the range to the array's real bounds would handle that case directly.

How would you handle multiple different keys k applied to the same array in different queries? Precomputing prefix sums over the doubled array once would let each query be answered in O(1) instead of O(n * k) every time.
The circular wraparound technique (index modulo n, corrected for negative values) reappears in any problem involving a circular array or circular buffer.
The "normalize a signed parameter into a direction and magnitude" idea is a general simplification technique, useful whenever a problem's behavior depends symmetrically on the sign of some input.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * k) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (normalized direction and steps): O(n * k) time, O(n) space (same complexity, simpler shared logic).

items: Pattern: Circular array neighbor summing, with direction and magnitude normalized from a signed key
Core Idea: Positive and negative k are mirror-image versions of the same "sum k neighbors" operation, so normalizing them into one direction and one step count avoids duplicated logic
Time: O(n * k)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Modulo arithmetic, corrected for negative values, is what makes indices correctly wrap around a circular array in either direction
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Normalize the sign into a direction, then step and wrap the same way every time
